headlines.title: Democrat Xavier Becerra wins California governor's race, defeating Republican Steve Hilton
headlines.description: Xavier Becerra, a Democrat who ran on his decades of experience in public office, will take over from California Gov. Gavin Newsom as the next governor of the nation’s most populous state. The victory by Becerra, a former state attorney general and Biden administration official, ensures California and the White House will remain adversaries for the final two years of President Donald Trump’s second term. Becerra repeatedly tied his opponent, Republican Steve Hilton, to the president and promised to defend California against Trump’s policies on everything from immigration to voting rights. “If anyone wants to come after California or any one Californian, they better be ready for a fight,” Becerra said Tuesday night in front of a crowd near Sacramento. Becerra argued he was best positioned for the job after serving more than 35 years in state and federal office, including as a congressman and health secretary in President Joe Biden’s administration. Hilton, a former Fox News host and adviser to former U.K. Prime Minister David Cameron, has never held elected office. Becerra will be California’s first Latino governor since the late 19th century. He sustained Democrats’ 16-year winning streak in statewide California elections, which Hilton tried to break by arguing one-party rule was to blame for the state’s high cost of living and homelessness crisis. He argued Becerra would prolong his party’s failure to adequately address homelessness. “This is what you get with one-party rule,” Hilton said at a news conference before Election Day. “You get a bunch of people in charge who think that they can get away with anything.” He said after losing to Becerra that “the change we hoped for may be delayed, but the change is coming.” The state Democratic leadership is likely to face greater scrutiny if Newsom, who was barred from seeking a third term, embarks on a bid for the presidency. A chaotic primary gave way to a low-key general election matchup The two candidates emerged from a large primary field with half a dozen prominent Democrats and two notable Republicans. Becerra wasn’t considered a top contender for the first months of his campaign. He admitted at a recent rally that his campaign was “an afterthought, maybe even a punchline” at the time. That changed when former Democratic Rep. Eric Swalwell, who had been viewed as a front-runner, dropped out of the race and resigned from Congress following allegations he sexually assaulted several women. He’s denied the accusations. His departure caused the party establishment and voters to look for a more reliable alternative, and they found one in Becerra. He sought to take advantage of Trump’s deep unpopularity in the state by tying Hilton to Trump, noting the president has endorsed the Republican. Becerra’s campaign launched a website that lists quotes of Hilton expressing support for the president and his policies. The site includes illustrations of the two Republicans standing side by side. Hilton tried to break through by releasing splashy ads, sometimes with AI-generated content, to encourage voters who typically choose Democrats to try something new. He also tried to appeal to the public by making ambitious promises, including pledging to abolish the DMV and cut gas prices to $3 a gallon, a rate the state hasn’t seen in years. Becerra will be state’s 1st Latino governor in over a century Becerra was born in Sacramento to a mother from Mexico and a father who was born in California and raised in Mexico. He’s made appealing to Latino voters a key part of his campaign strategy, including by releasing ads and social media posts in Spanish. “I’m running to be what the haters fear most: a proud son of immigrants with a law degree and a union card governing America’s most diverse and successful state,” Becerra said at a recent rally.

headlines.title: Teen faces murder charges in Fairfield Halloween store mass shooting
headlines.description: A 17-year-old Solano County teen is facing murder and attempted murder charges following a deadly mass shooting last Friday night at a Fairfield Halloween store. The 17-year-old suspect was arrested Monday at his family’s Suisun City home. A spokesperson for the Fairfield Police Department said it did not take long to identify the suspected shooter. “After reviewing surveillance footage from the store, the school resource officer recognized the suspect as a former student and provided that information to the detectives,” said Michelle Belyea of the Fairfield Police Department. Fairfield Police Chief Dan Marshall said the teenager had an ongoing dispute with one of the six other victims who were wounded in the mass shooting at the Spirit Halloween store located at the Solano Town Center Mall. Marshall also noted that the teen suspect was previously released from a juvenile detention center after serving just a few months for a shooting in a high school parking lot in 2025, though nobody was injured in that crime. Voicing his frustration over the repeat offense, Chief Marshall asked, “How many more people need to get shot or killed before we start making some changes? We need to hold kids accountable.” The big question at this hour is whether the teenage suspect will face these murder and attempted murder charges as a juvenile or be prosecuted as an adult and face life in prison. Steven Clark, a Bay Area legal analyst, said it is very likely the Solano County District Attorney’s Office is considering charging the teen as an adult, though a judge will have the final say. “If this goes to adult court, this young man could be facing the rest of his life in jail. If it stays in juvenile court, he’s likely to be released in his mid-twenties,” Clark said. Constance Hages, a 31-year-old pregnant mother of four, was killed in the shooting. Her aunt posted on Facebook that the family is grieving and trying to raise money through a GoFundMe page to help support her niece’s children and pay for “homegoing” services. Clark added that the judge deciding whether the teen will be tried as an adult will likely listen to victim and family statements before making a final decision. “…and obviously, the most important factor will be the severity of this crime. Certainly, the victim impact statements, to the court, will be very moving and telling, and I think it will be difficult for the court not to move this case to adult court,” Clark said. NBC Bay Area reached out to the Solano County District Attorney’s Office for further comment regarding charges and motives, but they have not yet responded.

headlines.title: UC Berkeley student arrested by ICE at SFO Airport
headlines.description: A UC Berkeley student remains in federal custody after being arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement at San Francisco International Airport on Friday. Paula Valentina Hernandez, 23, was taken into custody while waiting to board a flight to Portland for a vacation with her boyfriend. Agency records show she is currently being held at ICE’s California City Detention Center. The arrest has drawn a swift response from the campus community. UC Berkeley students and administration are mobilizing to support Hernandez.

headlines.title: Bay Area voter guide: What to know about the November 2026 election
headlines.description: What to Know — Election Day is Nov. 3, 2026 California will choose a new governor to replace Gavin Newsom, who terms out after this year. The choices are Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton. Voters will decide 14 state propositions. Regional sales tax Measure RTM, the Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative, aims to increase funds for public transit. California’s Congressional District 11 race features Scott Wiener and Connie Chan competing to succeed Nancy Pelosi. Aisha Wahab and Melissa Hernandez will face off again after a special election in August where Wahab secured victory to serve the remainder of former California U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell’s term. All 80 California Assembly seats are up for reelection, as well as 20 Senate seats. California’s general election is Nov. 3, with statewide races and propositions as well as key local races and measures across the Bay Area. Here’s what you need to know to cast your ballot, including important dates and deadlines, how to register or check your status, where and when to vote, and what’s on the ballot. In this guide: Key election dates Check voter registration status How to register to vote How to find your polling place What to bring to your polling place How to track your mail-in ballot Why is California choosing a new governor? 14 California propositions What to watch Alameda County What to watch Contra Costa County What to watch Napa County What to watch San Francisco What to watch San Mateo County What to watch Santa Clara County What to watch Solano County County election offices Key election dates The last day to register to vote for the Nov. 3 general election is Oct. 19. County election officials will start mailing ballots by Oct. 5. Ballot drop-off locations open on Oct. 6 Last day to register to vote for the general election is Oct. 19. First vote centers open for early in-person voting in all Voter’s Choice Act counties on Oct. 24. In person early voting locations in the state open on Oct. 31. Election Day, Nov. 3, is the last day to vote in-person or return a ballot by 8 p.m. Polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Vote-by-mail ballots must be postmarked no later than Nov. 3. If mailing on election day, get a hand-stamped postmark from a postal employee inside a post office. Visit the California Secretary of State’s website for a full list of key dates and deadlines. Check voter registration status Voters can check their registration at voterstatus.sos.ca.gov to confirm their mailing address and voting status. How to register to vote California residents can register to vote in elections at registertovote.ca.gov. Note Oct. 19 is the last day to register for the general election. Same day voter registration window will be open from Oct. 20 up to the Nov. 3 election day. Visit caearlyvoting.sos.ca.gov for a list of early voting locations to complete same day registration. How to find your polling place Visit the California Secretary of State’s website, where you can input your address to find your polling location and see what is on your ballot. Voters can also visit their county elections office for more information. Scroll down to the Bay Area county election offices section of this guide for further contact information. What to bring to your polling place Voters usually are not required to show identification to a polling place worker before casting a ballot, according to the Secretary of State’s website. There are some instances when providing identification is required: Voting for the first time after registering to vote by mail and did not provide a driver license number California identification number or the last four digits of social security number are missing on registration form In these cases voters should plan to bring identification to a polling place or bring a copy of it with their vote-by-mail ballot. The Secretary of State says the following are acceptable forms of identification: Passport Driver license Official state identification card Student identification card Copy of recent utility bill Sample ballot booklet received from county elections office Any document received by a government agency How to track your mail-in ballot Voters can track their vote-by-mail ballot and confirm it has been received by using the state’s Where’s My Ballot? tool at california.ballottrax.net/voter/. Ballots mailed in may take a few days to appear on the website. Why is California choosing a new governor? Gov. Gavin Newsom terms out after this year and voters will choose between Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton, who both advanced to the general election after a wild primary. Becerra has served as former President Joe Biden’s top health official and oversaw the response to the coronavirus pandemic. He was also the California’s attorney general during President Donald Trump’s first term and has more than two decades of experience as a congressmember. Hilton was a conservative commentator with a show on Fox News for six years. He also worked as an adviser to former British prime minister David Cameron. What are the 14 California propositions voters will decide in the November election? Here’s a list of the California propositions on the November ballot. Use the expandable graphic below for a breakdown on what to know about each measure. 2026 California Ballot Propositions Click on a proposition to see more information about what will happen if it does or doesn’t pass. Source: NBC Staff Reports • Interactive: Annetta Stogniew Regional measure to watch Measure RTM: The Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative, is a regional sales tax aimed at increasing funds for public transit. It includes 5 Bay Area counties: Alameda, Contra Costa, San Francisco, San Mateo, and Santa Clara. Races and measures to watch in Alameda County California Congressional District 14: California lawmaker Aisha Wahab and Bay Area Rapid Transit Director Melissa Hernandez will face off again to determine who will serve the next full two-year term. Wahab topped Hernandez in an August special election to serve the remainder of former California U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell’s term. Swalwell resigned from Congress earlier this year after sexual assault and misconduct allegations. District 14 includes the East Bay cities such as Fremont, Hayward and Livermore. Measure X in Berkeley: Would establish 10% limit on annual rent increases and other changes to the city’s rent ordinance. Measure Y in Berkeley: Parcel tax to pay for arts projects. Measure Z in Berkeley: Parcel tax to fund a public bank. Measure AA in Berkeley: Increase soda tax Measure EE in Oakland: Shift city to a strong mayor system. Measure FF in Oakland: Eliminate foreclosure exemption from property transfer tax. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Alameda County and additional election information, visit the Alameda County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Contra Costa County In Contra Costa County, several county board of education seats are open. In Richmond, residents will vote on a new mayor while voters in San Pablo will weigh in on Measure S, which would limit rent increases. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Contra Costa County and additional election information, visit the Contra Costa County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Napa County California Congressional District 4: Mike Thompson faces Eric Jones. Measure B in Napa County: Sales tax to fund wildfire prevention and open space preservation. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Napa County and additional election information, visit the Napa County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in San Francisco San Francisco voters will weigh in on several open seats on the county board of supervisors and board of education. Proposition A: Give mayor more power to hire and fire department heads. Proposition B: Pave way for public bank. Proposition C: Increase the city’s annual contribution to an affordable housing trust fund. Proposition D: New barriers to placing measures on the ballot. Proposition E: Changes to city contracting. Proposition G: Reopen parts of the Great Highway to vehicle traffic on weekdays. Proposition H: Parcel tax to fund Muni. Proposition J: Eliminate foreclosure exemption from property transfer tax California Congressional District 11: Scott Wiener and Connie Chan compete to succeed Nancy Pelosi. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in San Francisco and additional election information, visit the San Francisco Department of Elections website. Races and measures to watch in San Mateo County Measure E in Redwood City: Limit rent increases. Measure Q in Half Moon Bay: Referendum to block proposed farmworker housing. Measure U in San Mateo County: Create independent commission to draw supervisor districts. For a complete list of San Mateo County measures and races on the ballot, visit smacre.gov/elections. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in San Mateo County and additional election information, visit the San Mateo County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Santa Clara County In San Jose, incumbents Peter Ortiz and Bien Doan are up for re-election in Districts 5 and 7, respectively, and there’s an open seat in District 9. Races and measures to watch in Solano County Solano County Board of Supervisors, District 4: Mike Silva and John Carli face in a runoff in a district covering Vacaville and Dixon. Races and measures to watch in Sonoma County California Congressional District 1: Mike McGuire will face James Gallagher in a seat redistricted by Proposition 50. headlines.title: Bay Area rent check: Median price for 1-bedroom apartment in SF up to $4,400
headlines.description: The latest Bay Area rent numbers are out and, to probably no one’s surprise, prices are going up. New figures from rent tracker Zumper show San Francisco setting new records with the median monthly price for a one-bedroom apartment now above $4,400. The median rent for a two-bedroom apartment in San Francisco recently topped $6,000 for the first time ever. Rent is on the rise anywhere tech companies are hiring. “The markets closest to any tech and AI job center will see a lot more demand and will push rents up,” Zumper’s Crystal Chen said. NBC Bay Area’s Scott Budman has more in the video report above. This story uses functionality that may not work in our app. Click here to open the story in your web browser.

headlines.title: Election Day: Here's what's at stake in the Bay Area as voters head to polls
headlines.description: Bay Area polls are open and voting is underway Tuesday for the November midterm election. California voters will choose a new governor to replace Gavin Newsom, who terms out after this year. The choices are Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton. From allocating funds aimed at boosting affordable housing to levying a tax on billionaires in the state, voters will also weigh in on 14 California propositions. Elections Sep 17 Decision 2026 Oct 2 There are also a host of key races in the Bay Area. The Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative is a regional sales tax aimed at increasing funds for public transit. It includes 5 Bay Area counties: Alameda, Contra Costa, San Francisco, San Mateo, and Santa Clara. Alameda County voters will choose between California lawmaker Aisha Wahab and Bay Area Rapid Transit Director Melissa Hernandez for who will serve the Congressional District 14’s next full two-year term. Oakland residents will also have their say on whether Barbara Lee will continue to serve as mayor. In Contra Costa County, several county board of education seats are open. In Richmond, residents will vote on a new mayor while voters in San Pablo will weigh in on Measure S, which would limit rent increases. San Francisco voters are considering several propositions, including Prop B, which would pave the way for a public bank, and Prop G, which would reopen parts of the Great Highway to vehicle traffic on weekdays. Prop H if passed would establish a parcel tax to fund Muni. City voters will also weigh in on the Congressional District 11 race, where Scott Wiener and Connie Chan compete to succeed Nancy Pelosi. In San Mateo County, Measure E in Redwood City would limit rent increases. Measure Q in Half Moon Bay would block proposed farmworker housing and Measure U aims to create an independent commission to draw supervisor districts in the county. In San Jose, incumbents Peter Ortiz and Bien Doan are up for re-election in Districts 5 and 7, respectively, and there’s an open seat in District 9. South Bay residents will also vote in mayoral races held in Milpitas, Morgan Hill and Santa Clara. Marin County County voters will decide on several measures related to paramedic and emergency medical services. City council seats are also up for election in Novato, San Rafael, Larkspur and Sausalito. In Solano County, voters will choose between Mike Silva and John Carli, who will face in a runoff for a supervisors district covering Vacaville and Dixon. Measure E if passed by voters would establish a tax on data centers and battery storage facilities in the unincorporated county areas. Sonoma County voters will decide whether Mike McGuire or James Gallagher takes a seat redistricted by Proposition 50.

headlines.title: It's too early to call the outcome of California's proposal to tax billionaires
headlines.description: A California measure to tax the net worth of billionaires that divided liberal leaders nationally and triggered one of the most expensive ballot fights in state history was too early to call Wednesday morning as the vote tally continued. Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of Californians whose net worth exceeds $1 billion, with most of the revenue dedicated to replacing federal funding cuts to healthcare. The measure left the ultra-rich, some of whom spent heavily to defeat it, scrambling to figure out whether they would pay the tax or leave California. Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders framed the proposal as a monumental step toward reining in deep wealth inequality by ensuring the ultra-rich pay their fair share. But Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom warned it would prompt the state’s wealthiest to move out of California and take their tax money with them. With almost 6 million votes yet to be counted, the AP Decision Team will wait for additional vote results before declaring a winner. Opponents of the proposed one-time tax on billionaires have outnumbered supporters across most of the state. “No” has sizable leads in the Inland/Central Valley region and the San Diego and Orange County area, and smaller leads along the central coast and in the Bay Area. “Yes” votes led narrowly in Los Angeles County and the northern coast. The “no” side raised roughly 10 times as much as the “yes” side, thanks in large part to tech moguls and venture capitalists, who poured millions into a political action committee fighting the measure. Some billionaires, including Google co-founders Sergey Brin and Larry Page, started cutting ties with the state in anticipation of the proposed tax. Mark Zuckerberg said he would stay in California for eight years and made a deal with Meta that would help him pay the tax without losing his ownership stake in the company. Backers of the proposed tax, led by the powerful labor union SEIU United Healthcare Workers West, said it was needed to help the state backfill the federal funding cuts. The union estimates the state will lose $100 billion in federal healthcare funding over five years. “It’s time to collect those taxes so we can ensure that our healthcare system is still safe,” said Lorena Gonzalez, president of the California Federation of Labor Unions. But some traditional Democratic allies, including Planned Parenthood and the California Teachers Association, are part of a coalition that opposed it. They’re concerned about how the tax revenue would be divvied up and about the potential impact on the state’s budget if there’s a mass exodus of wealthy taxpayers. California’s budget relies heavily on the income tax of the state’s richest residents. Robert Swonger, an auto glass technician living near Sacramento who’s politically independent, said he planned to vote against it. “Obviously, I would like billionaires not to have as much money as they do,” he said. “But I don’t believe taxing them out of existence is going to work.” Anthony Serrano, a Democrat living in Folsom who works for Kaiser Permanente, one of the nation’s largest not-for-profit healthcare plans, said he was leaning toward voting for the tax because he tends to support “anything that is a positive for healthcare.” Even if the measure wins approval from a majority of voters, it would be blocked from taking effect if at least one of two measures designed to nullify it — Propositions 41 and 42 — passes and receives more “yes” votes. The proposals, which are backed by the political action committee Building a Better California, include a ban on new taxes on financial assets and other personal property, a category that excludes real estate. The committee raised more than $333 million, about 30% of it from Brin. Progressive politicians, including Sanders and Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren, have long supported a federal wealth tax. Newsom said a California wealth tax would disadvantage the state, but he supports a national minimum tax on anyone with a net worth above $100 million. Days before Sanders held rallies in California cities last month urging voters to support the state measure, Newsom told reporters that the senator’s focus on wealth inequality was “spot-on.” But he said that “on this issue, we fundamentally disagree.” Even if the proposed billionaire tax fails in California, the battle over the measure ignited a crucial dialogue on the issue, Gonzalez said. “We are taking a step forward, and we are showing other states that you can look them in the eye — you can look these billionaires in the eye — and take them on,” she said.

headlines.title: Bay Area transit agencies add service to get fans to Valkyries' parade in San Francisco
headlines.description: Bay Area transit agencies are preparing for large crowds Wednesday as fans head to San Francisco to celebrate the Golden State Valkyries’ historic WNBA championship with a parade at noon. The Valkyries captured their first WNBA championship after defeating the Atlanta Dream 68-63 in Game 7 of the Finals at Chase Center on Saturday, becoming the first expansion team in the league to win a championship in their second season. Caltrain, BART and SamTrans are encouraging fans to take public transportation to avoid traffic and parking challenges during the celebration. Caltrain will run two additional special trains for the parade. The northbound train 901 will leave San Jose Diridon Station at 9:13 a.m., making all regular stops before reaching San Francisco. After the parade, the southbound train 902 will leave San Francisco Station at 2:40 p.m. and make local stops. Caltrain will also run two afternoon trains as locals to handle crowds. Train 914 will depart San Francisco at 3:10 p.m., followed by train 916 at 3:40 p.m. Riders traveling south of Tamien Station can connect to those trains through services 814 and 816. Fans can walk from Caltrain’s San Francisco station to the parade’s end at 2nd and King streets or head along the Embarcadero toward the starting point at the Ferry Building. Golden State Valkyries Nov 1 Golden State Valkyries Nov 2 Golden State Valkyries Nov 2 BART, meanwhile, will run extra trains, longer trains and add staff and security for the event. Riders can take BART to Embarcadero or Montgomery stations and walk to the parade. Another option is to take BART to Powell Street Station and transfer to Muni’s southbound T Third train at Union Square Station, then get off at 4th and King streets and walk to the parade. SamTrans also offers several routes connecting the Peninsula to downtown San Francisco. Route 292 serves communities in San Mateo County and connects to the Salesforce Transit Center. The FCX and EPX routes also serve the transit center during peak periods. Fans can also take Route 292 or Route ECR to Millbrae Station and transfer to Caltrain for service to San Francisco, SamTrans officials said. The three transit agencies are advising riders to check schedules and real-time updates before leaving.

headlines.title: Testimony slated to start in retrial of Sierra LaMar murder case
headlines.description: Testimony in the retrial of the man accused of killing Morgan Hill teenager Sierra LaMar is expected to start Tuesday. LaMar disappeared on her way to her bus stop before school in 2012. Five years later, Antolin Garcia-Torres was found guilty in her murder, but that decision was later overturned by an appellate court because the district attorney’s office introduced three unrelated kidnapping accusations against him. During opening statements Monday, the Santa Clara County prosecutor tried to paint a picture of the day LaMar disappeared in March 2012. He explained that even though LaMar has not been found, there is evidence connecting LaMar and Garcia-Torres. He said carpet fibers from Garcia-Torres’ car were found on LaMar’s clothing and her DNA and a strand of her hair her found in the trunk. “Sierra’s body has never been found, yet traces of Sierra were found in the car driven by that man right there,” prosecutor O’Bryan Kenney said, pointing at Garcia-Torres. “Traces of that man were found on Sierra‘s clothes. Traces of that man’s car were found on Sierra’s clothes.” Garcia-Torres’ attorney said it was all evidence that was mishandled. “You want to carefully handle the items so that you don’t cross-contaminate or contaminate these items because you’re mishandling the evidence,” defense attorney Al Lopez said. “There’s protocols for this, and you’re going to see they weren’t followed.” Lopez also told the jury that they would be hearing about someone else who could’ve been involved. The trial is expected to resume at 9 a.m. Tuesday and stretch into next year. Morgan Hill Nov 2 Morgan Hill Oct 2 Sierra LaMar murder case: Judge will not recuse himself, jury selection next week
